groups.summary: I reproduced all six members on Python 3.13.16 with websockets 14.1, using my own fake CDP peer and also real headless Chromium 141. Three things go wrong. (1) When Transaction.__call__ fails to parse a reply, the exception escapes Listener.listener_loop at the `tx(**message)` call, which has no try around it. The listener dies, and the Transaction it already popped from mapper is never resolved: send() hangs forever, and neither later sends nor aclose() release it. (2) An async handler whose arity is wrong raises TypeError synchronously in the callback dispatch. The code logs it and then re-raises on purpose, which kills the listener. (3) Any exception from _receive_message other than TimeoutError, CancelledError or ConnectionClosed (JSONDecodeError, KeyError, ConcurrencyError) also kills the listener without logging anything. In cases (2) and (3) the tx stays in mapper, so an in-flight send hangs until some later send() starts a new Listener. Once the browser connection's listener is dead, every send from a flat-session tab hangs: Tab.aopen/_attach_session returns early and never revives the parent's listener, so nobody reads the shared websocket.

member_verdicts.note: Fake peer sends a non-JSON text frame before the Browser.getVersion reply. Listener exc is JSONDecodeError, nothing is logged, and send stays pending after 3s with mapper=[1]. Stuck at connection.py:662 send `return await tx`. A malformed Target.detachedFromTarget with no params.sessionId gives KeyError('sessionId') from _receive_message with the same hang. A second reader on the websocket (artificial setup) kills the listener with ConcurrencyError. Refinement: the tx stays in mapper, so the hang ends at the next send() on that connection (that run printed 'original done=True result=P'). I found no natural trigger in zendriver for the ConcurrencyError or the non-JSON frame, so the triggers are defensive / low realism even though the mechanism is real.

Target.getTargetInfo answered with result={} gives listener exc KeyError('targetInfo'), mapper size 0, and send not done after 3s. The same happens for a reply with no 'result' key (KeyError('result')) and for Storage.getCookies with sameSite 'SomeFutureValue' (ValueError("'SomeFutureValue' is not a valid CookieSameSite")). A later get_version works because a new listener is created, but the original send is still pending. I did not test the claim that _inbox piles up.

Runtime.evaluate with exceptionDetails {'bogus':1} gives KeyError('exceptionId'). A custom generator doing `return j['x']` gives KeyError('x') and hangs on the fake peer. On real Chromium a tab custom generator hung 5s instead of raising KeyError('notThere'), with tab mapper size 0. A generator that yields twice reaches the explicit `raise ProtocolException('could not parse...')`, which also kills the listener. The secondary claim holds too: Connection.wait() (t=None) called while events stream stays blocked >4s at connection.py:579 `await self.listener.idle.wait()` after the bad reply kills that listener.

In all 6 parse-failure variants the send was still pending after a later successful send AND after conn.aclose() ('after aclose(): original send done=False'). The tx had been popped, so _fail_pending_transactions cannot see it. A good reply queued right behind the bad one (cmd2) also hung 3s with mapper=[2]. Zendriver logged nothing at WARNING or above.

Registering `async def bad_handler()` with zero parameters for TargetCreated, followed by a good handler, then sending a TargetCreated event before the getVersion reply: TypeError, a warning is logged, the listener dies, the good handler never fires (fired=[]), and get_version hangs 3s. The next send revives the listener and the old send completes. The next event kills the listener again ('second round' hung). Refinements: the error is logged as a warning, so it is not silent. It only applies to coroutine-function handlers. A sync handler with the wrong arity goes through asyncio.to_thread, so the error surfaces as 'Task exception was never retrieved' and the listener keeps running.

Fake peer with a SimpleNamespace owner: after the browser listener died (KeyError('nope')), two successive tab.send(Runtime.evaluate) calls each hung 3s. The tab listener was running, inbox size 0, browser listener not running, and the peer did receive the session-scoped commands. One browser-level send fixed it (value 4). Real Chromium 141 shows the same: tab.evaluate('2+2') hung 8s at tab.py:859 evaluate -> send. After browser.connection.send(get_targets()) it finished with value 4, while the browser-level tx that was lost stayed pending.

groups.refinements: Failure modes split by duration. Parse failures in Transaction.__call__ (A1.1/A2.3/B15.1) lose the tx permanently: it was popped from mapper, and neither later sends nor aclose() resolve it; only cancelling the caller ends it. Handler-raise (B15.4) and _receive_message exceptions (SEED-L1) leave the tx in mapper, so the in-flight send recovers at the next send() on that same connection (or fails at aclose). For a flat-session tab whose parent browser listener died (A2.4), tab sends do not help: only a browser-level send revives it. B15.4 applies only to coroutine-function handlers and is logged as a warning. SEED-L1 is silent, but I found no natural trigger for the ConcurrencyError or a non-JSON frame. Its realistic value is defensive, so its realism is lower than the parse-failure path, which has a historical Chrome-skew precedent (#245). Connection.wait() without t also hangs forever if the listener dies while idle is clear. Not tested: _inbox growth while a tab listener is dead.

groups.summary:
I could not refute this group. Every member's mechanism reproduces on Python 3.13 and websockets 14.1, using a fake CDP peer, real headless Chromium 141, or both.

(1) Transaction.__call__ lets any non-StopIteration exception from the generated parser or a custom generator escape. The Listener.listener_loop call `tx(**message)` has no try around it, so the listener task dies. The Transaction was already popped from mapper, so its future is never resolved, and aclose()/_fail_pending_transactions cannot release it. The send() hangs permanently.

(2) In the listener_loop callback dispatch, the `raise` after logger.warning, plus the outer `except Exception: raise`, kill the listener when an async handler with the wrong arity is called.

(3) A flat-session Tab's aopen/_attach_session returns early once session_id is set. Its send() restarts only the tab's own inbox Listener. When browser.connection.listener is dead, nothing reads the shared websocket, and every tab command hangs until something sends on the browser connection.

(4) Any other exception from _receive_message (for example a JSONDecodeError) also kills the listener. I found no way for real Chrome to trigger this in the current code.

member_verdicts.note: Mechanism confirmed with a fake peer (probe_recv.py). A non-JSON text frame kills the listener with JSONDecodeError and the in-flight send hangs. The only trace is 'Task exception was never retrieved' at GC. Two refinements. (a) The tx stays in mapper, so aclose() fails it with ProtocolException('connection was closed'), and a later send() starts a new Listener that delivers replies still in the buffer. The hang is permanent only when the lost frame was itself the reply. (b) No real-Chrome trigger found. The ConcurrencyError route (the aopen race) is fixed on this branch by commit 31c92f1 (_open_lock), and I found no other way to get two concurrent recv() calls. Chrome caps reply nesting at about 300 levels (verified), below the json.loads RecursionError depth: about 976 on Python 3.11, about 9995 on 3.12/3.13. Chrome escapes lone surrogates (verified). Invalid UTF-8 becomes ConnectionClosed, which the loop already handles. Realism with real Chrome is low; a non-Chrome CDP endpoint or proxy that sends non-JSON frames could reach it.

Fake peer (probe_parse.py): Target.getTargetInfo answered with result {} -> send() hangs, listener exception KeyError('targetInfo'), mapper {}. Storage.getCookies with sameSite 'SomeFutureValue' -> ValueError and the same hang. A reply with no 'result' key -> KeyError('result') and the same hang. Other in-flight commands hang only until a later send() revives the listener: their replies are still buffered and they are still in mapper (verified in the concurrent case). The explicit raise ProtocolException('could not parse') is reachable only from a custom generator that yields twice; generated commands always end with StopIteration. On Chromium 141 with the bundled cdp, none of the 40 common command replies I tried failed to parse (verified), so the trigger needs Chrome/protocol skew. Git history shows such skew does happen: f9b442b, Chrome 146 dropped cookie sameParty and browser.cookies.get_all() broke. Note that cookies.get_all() sends on the first open tab, so that case kills only the tab listener, not the browser one.

Real Chromium (real_tab_flows.py): a custom generator returning j['notThere'] -> tab.send() hung for 5s and the tab listener died, stuck at Connection.send `return await tx`. The next tab.evaluate worked because send() restarts the tab Listener. Fake peer: KeyError from the custom generator gives the same hang. The tab.wait() sub-claim is confirmed with a fake peer (probe_wait.py): a wait() already blocked on the dead listener's idle event never returns. A new wait() does return, because its update_target send revives the listener. Realism for the custom-generator path is low to medium, since the send() docstring invites custom commands.

Fake peer: after the parse failure, conn.aclose() leaves the send pending (verified for all five parse-failure variants), because the tx was popped from mapper before tx(**message). On the browser connection this also starves every flat-session tab; see A2.4, verified with real Chrome. Parse errors in events are caught and logged (parse_json_event try/except), which shows the intended behaviour is to log and carry on. CHANGELOG entries such as 'listener crashing with InvalidStateError ... left later commands hanging forever' show maintainers treat listener death as a bug, not a design choice. No test asserts the current behaviour.

Fake peer (probe_handler.py): the listener dies only for async callables whose call raises synchronously: `async def h()`, `async def h(a,b,c)`, or functools.partial(async_f, extra). Sync functions and lambdas with the wrong arity do not kill it (they go through asyncio.to_thread and fail in their own task). Exceptions raised inside a handler body do not kill it. Neither does an instance with an async __call__ (it takes the to_thread route). Real Chromium (verified): with `async def on_request(): pass` on tab RequestWillBeSent, `tab.send(cdp.page.navigate(url))` hung for 8s, because Chrome sends the event before the navigate reply. tab.get(url) is bounded: it raises TimeoutError after 10s because of the wait_for inside Tab.get. With the same kind of handler on browser.connection for TargetInfoChanged, a tab navigation killed the browser listener. The in-flight send recovers once a later send revives the listener, but each new matching event kills it again. A warning is logged, so the user does get a hint. Realism is medium, since this is a common user mistake.

Real Chromium (real_tabs.py, verified): after the browser listener died (TypeError from a wrong-arity TargetInfoChanged handler on browser.connection), tab.evaluate('2+2') and tab.send(runtime.evaluate) each hung for 5s. The stack was at Tab.evaluate -> Connection.send `return await tx`. The tab listener was running and its inbox was empty. After `browser.connection.send(cdp.target.get_targets())` the browser listener came back and tab.evaluate returned 8. Nothing in zendriver sends on the browser connection in the background, so tabs recover only when user code makes a browser-level call (update_targets, get(new_tab=True), and so on). The browser listener does the json.loads for every frame, including those routed to sessions, so any SEED-L1 exception there also starves all tabs.

groups.refinements:
- Parse-failure hangs (A1.1/A2.3/B15.1) are permanent for the affected send: the tx was popped from mapper, so aclose() cannot fail it, and only the caller's own timeout ends the wait. Other in-flight commands are stuck only until the next send() on the same connection.

- B15.4 applies only to async callables (including partials of them) whose call raises synchronously. A hang needs a command whose reply is queued behind the triggering event. Tab.get is bounded at 10s.
- A2.4 is an amplifier: any death of the browser listener, from a handler, a skewed browser-level reply, or an unexpected receive exception, starves all tabs until a browser-level send.
- SEED-L1 has no real-Chrome trigger in the current code: the ConcurrencyError route was fixed by 31c92f1, nesting is capped by Chrome, and surrogates are escaped. The tx stays in mapper, so aclose() and later sends recover it unless the lost frame was the reply itself.
- The behaviour is not Python-version dependent; the RecursionError path is the only one that would be, and Chrome cannot reach it.

groups.summary: Confirmed: all four listener-robustness defects are real, and each needs its own fix. (1) Transaction.__call__ (connection.py ~L112-130) catches only StopIteration. A KeyError or ValueError from a generated from_json, an exception from a custom generator, or its own explicit `raise ProtocolException('could not parse...')` escapes through `tx(**message)` in Listener.listener_loop (~L973), which is outside every try. The listener dies, and the tx was already popped from mapper, so send() hangs forever and aclose() cannot release it. (2) Callback dispatch in listener_loop (~L1000-1011) logs a handler that raises when called (e.g. wrong arity) and then re-raises, which kills the listener. (3) The receive try in listener_loop catches only TimeoutError, CancelledError and ConnectionClosed. Any other exception from _receive_message (e.g. JSONDecodeError, RuntimeError/ConcurrencyError) ends the task silently and in-flight sends hang. (4) For a flat-session tab, Connection.aopen only calls _attach_session, which returns early once session_id is set. Nothing restarts the browser connection's listener, so every tab command hangs after that listener stops. The minimal local fix has 4 hunks and passes: 9 regression tests fail (hang) on the repo and pass on the prototype, on both Python 3.13 and 3.11. 68 of the repo's own tests also pass against the prototype with real headless Chromium, and mypy shows no new errors.

member_verdicts.note: Fake websocket on py3.13: one non-JSON frame, or recv() raising RuntimeError, in front of the Browser.getVersion reply. Repo: listener task done with JSONDecodeError('Expecting value...'); send() stuck at connection.py:662 `return await tx`; tx still in mapper. Realism low: Chrome does not send non-JSON, and websockets ConcurrencyError needs a second concurrent recv(), which zendriver's Listener bookkeeping avoids. Fix hunk 3 (log, fail pending tx of the connection and its flat sessions, break) makes send raise, and the next send works. A 'log and continue' variant is unsafe: on py3.13 wait_for runs the coroutine inline, so a persistent error raised before the first suspension (ConcurrencyError) spins without yielding. probe_continue_freeze.py: 'FROZEN: event loop made no progress for 3s (heartbeat ticks 1)' vs prototype 'heartbeat ticked 50 times in ~0.5s'.

Fake peer answers Target.getTargetInfo with result {} -> repo: send hangs, listener exc KeyError('targetInfo'), mapper {}. Storage.getCookies with a cookie whose sameSite is 'SomeFutureValue' -> hangs, ValueError. Prototype: raises ProtocolException('could not parse the cdp response...') with __cause__ set; the same listener object keeps running and the next send works. Real-world precedent: commit f9b442b 'Fix crash in browser.cookies.get_all() on Chrome 146 when the sameParty field is missing' is exactly this class of protocol skew.

Custom generator `j = yield {...Runtime.evaluate...}; return j['notThere']`. Fake peer: repo hangs, listener exc KeyError('notThere'). Real headless Chromium 141 via tab.send (flat session): repo 'HUNG (> 5s)' plus 'Task exception was never retrieved ... Listener.listener_loop ... KeyError('notThere')'; prototype 'raised ProtocolException'. Ablation shows this site is separate from SEED-L1: with only the receive-side except added, the parse tests still hang, because tx(**message) is outside that try.

Same root cause as A1.1/A2.3. The extra claim was checked too. probe_aclose.py on repo: 'before aclose: done False | mapper {}' then 'after aclose: send finished? False'. aclose()/_fail_pending_transactions cannot reach the popped tx. Prototype: tx already failed with ProtocolException. The explicit 'could not parse' raise (generator that yields twice) also hung on repo, and now gives ProtocolException via set_exception.

Fake peer sends Target.targetCreated and then the Browser.getVersion reply. Handlers registered: `async def bad(): pass` then a good one. Repo: send hangs, listener exc TypeError('...bad_handler() takes 0 positional arguments but 1 was given') raised at listener_loop line ~1000 after the warning log. Prototype (inner `raise` removed): send returns, listener running, good handler called once.

Browser-free: browser Connection plus a flat-session tab Connection (owner namespace). After the browser listener stops, the repo's tab.send hangs at connection.py:662. Real Chromium: a browser-level custom Target.getTargets whose parser raises -> 'browser listener running: False exc: notThere', then 'tab.evaluate after browser-level failure: HUNG (> 5s)'; prototype returns 4. Correction to the finder's repro: Runtime.evaluate on browser.connection gets a CDP error reply (no Runtime domain on the browser target), so it raises and does not kill the listener. A browser-domain command is needed. Once the other hunks are in, this path is reachable only through the receive-error break, but hunk 3 depends on it so that tabs recover.

groups.refinements: (a) The finder's real-Chrome repro for A2.4 (Runtime.evaluate custom cmd on browser.connection) does not hang, because Chrome answers with an error since the browser target has no Runtime domain. Use a browser-domain method (Target.getTargets) instead. (b) Severity is per path. For parse failures the tx is popped and lost, so the hang is permanent and aclose cannot release it. For the bad-handler and receive-error paths the tx stays in mapper, so a later send() (which restarts the listener) or aclose() releases it. For tabs it is permanent unless something sends on browser.connection. (c) The receive-error fix must break, not continue: a continue-based handler freezes the whole event loop on py>=3.12 when the error is persistent and synchronous (shown with ConcurrencyError). (d) Optional, not in the prototype: set self.idle on listener exit, so a wait() already blocked on the dead listener's idle event returns. This is pre-existing for ConnectionClosed too. Once hunk 1 is in, parse failures no longer kill the listener, which covers A2.3's tab.wait() side claim for that path. (e) The outer `except Exception: raise` in dispatch becomes dead code and can be dropped in the real PR.

fix_assessment.diff_summary: zendriver/core/connection.py only (full diff in Q1-fixsafety/prototype.diff). 1) Transaction.__call__: add `except Exception as e:` after `except StopIteration`, building ProtocolException('could not parse the cdp response:\n%s' % response), setting __cause__ = e, and `return self.set_exception(...)`. The trailing explicit `raise ProtocolException(...)` becomes `self.set_exception(ProtocolException(...))`. 2) Connection.aopen, flat-session branch, after `await self._attach_session(browser_connection)`: `if browser_connection.websocket is not None and (not browser_connection.listener or not browser_connection.listener.running): browser_connection.listener = Listener(browser_connection)`. 3) Listener.listener_loop receive try: add `except Exception as e:` after the ConnectionClosed clause. It logs a warning with exc_info, calls `session._fail_pending_transactions(e)` for each flat session and `self.connection._fail_pending_transactions(e)`, then `break`s; the next send() starts a new listener. 4) Listener.listener_loop callback dispatch: remove the `raise` after the per-callback logger.warning, so a faulty handler is logged and skipped.
fix_assessment.risks: No new locks, and no await between the check and the Listener() creation in hunk 2, so concurrent tab sends cannot start two readers on one websocket (no ConcurrencyError race). The check runs after _attach_lock is released, so there is no lock-ordering or re-entrancy problem. The websocket-not-None guard avoids starting a listener while the browser connection is opening (connect pending, websocket None) or after it is closed. CancelledError, KeyboardInterrupt and GeneratorExit are BaseException and stay uncaught. TimeoutError and ConnectionClosed clauses come first, so the new `except Exception` changes nothing for them. Behaviour changes callers would notice: (a) a parse failure now surfaces as ProtocolException (cause chained), not a hang. Callers that already catch ProtocolException (get_frames, _search_frames, describe_node loops, element resolve, _send_oneshot in _prepare_headless) now degrade gracefully. A custom generator that raises KeyError surfaces as ProtocolException(from KeyError), not KeyError. Setting the raw exception instead is the alternative, but it would bypass those handlers. (b) A handler that raises synchronously is logged at WARNING and the remaining handlers still run. (c) An unexpected receive error fails every in-flight command on that connection and its flat sessions with the raw exception (same style as the ConnectionClosed path). Tasks started by feed_cdp may then log 'exception never retrieved'. Replies still buffered are dropped as unknown ids when the listener restarts. Do not swap the break for continue: that freezes the event loop on py>=3.12 for persistent synchronous errors (demonstrated). Not addressed (pre-existing): a wait() already blocked on a stopped listener's idle event still hangs (setting idle on exit would fix it), and the parse-failure message embeds the full response, which may be large.

groups.summary: Confirmed on real headless Chromium (Python 3.13.16, scratch copy of the package). Tab.select/find/find_all/select_all/xpath/wait_for/__call__, cloudflare.cf_is_interactive_challenge_present and Tab.verify_cf all check their timeout only between CDP round trips. If the renderer never answers (an open alert(), or while(true){}), each call with timeout=2 was still pending after 8 s, and select and xpath were still pending after 30 s. Each one sits on an unbounded Transaction: DOM.getDocument, or DOM.enable for xpath. Under the same conditions the controls (wait_for_ready_state(timeout=2), already fixed in #291, and tab.wait(2)) returned after 2.00 s. If the renderer is busy for a finite 12 s, the same methods return 9 s late (11.2 to 11.7 s for timeout=2). Two smaller defects also reproduced. xpath(timeout<=0) never runs the query and returns [] even when the element exists, and with a positive timeout it spins with no sleep. verify_cf(timeout=1, click_delay=4) takes 4.02 s.

groups.refinements: The root cause matches the claim: each polling loop compares loop.time() with its deadline only after an awaited CDP round trip returns, and none of those awaits (DOM.getDocument in query_selector / query_selector_all / find_elements_by_text / cf_find_interactive_challenge, and DOM.enable in xpath) is bounded. In alert mode the hang is effectively forever: the Transaction stays pending as long as the dialog is open (seen for 30s). In finite-busy mode the deadline is overrun by the busy duration. Other observations: (a) the self.sleep -> update_target send (Target.getTargetInfo) never showed up as a blocking point, because the browser answers it even when the renderer is blocked; (b) Tab.__call__ passes its arguments to wait_for positionally in swapped order (text into selector), which is a separate bug that does not change the hang; (c) A11.4 and A5.7 are timing/contract bugs (wrong-result) rather than hangs, but they share the same files and would naturally be fixed together. A fix that wraps each polling body in asyncio.wait_for(remaining) must keep each method's documented outcome on timeout: TimeoutError for find, select, find_all, select_all, wait_for and verify_cf; [] for xpath; False for cf_is_interactive_challenge_present. The fix should also cancel the stuck Transaction cleanly.

groups.summary: I tried to refute this group and could not. On real headless Chromium 141 (--headless=new, Python 3.13), a JS alert() open in the tab means DOM.getDocument and DOM.enable never get a reply. Because of that, select, find, find_all, select_all (including include_frames), xpath, wait_for, tab(...), cf_is_interactive_challenge_present and verify_cf all stay pending far past timeout=2: I watched them for 12 s, and the Chrome behaviour behind it held for more than 34 s. Nothing upstream limits the wait. Headless does not auto-dismiss the dialog. The websocket stays up (PING_TIMEOUT=900). The Target.getTargetInfo call that Connection.sleep sends does get answered, so the hang is purely in the DOM sends. The most realistic trigger is a plain script: `tab = await browser.get(page that calls alert() while loading)` returns in 0.01 s, then `await tab.select('#a', timeout=3)` hangs forever even though #a exists. Commit bd88ccd (#291) already treated exactly this 'page stuck behind a dialog' case as a bug in wait_for_ready_state, and no test asserts the current behaviour. A busy main thread that eventually finishes only makes the calls late (an 8 s busy loop made every timeout=2 call finish at about 7.6 s with the documented result); only an infinite JS loop hangs. The two side members are also real: verify_cf can run past its timeout by up to click_delay, and xpath with timeout<=0 never runs the query and otherwise spins without sleeping.

Also reproduced in a plain script: browser.get(alert-on-load page) then select('#a', timeout=3) was still pending after 20 s. The sleep() -> update_target call is NOT a hang point, because Target.getTargetInfo is answered while the dialog is open (verified).

I only read the code for this, not tested.

With an alert open it hangs (verified, see B13.2). With an 8 s busy main thread, wait_for(timeout=2) raised TimeoutError only after 7.61 s. That is an overshoot limited by how long the page script runs, not a hang; only an infinite loop would hang.

groups.refinements:
1. A true hang needs a JS dialog (alert/confirm/prompt) open in the tab, or an infinite JS loop. Bounded busy JS only overshoots until the script yields; the result is still TimeoutError, [] or False, just late.
2. The trigger is page state, not a caller argument. The most realistic path is a page that alerts during load or from a timer: browser.get/tab.get return right away (about 0.01-0.12 s, verified), and the next select/find/wait_for hangs, even for elements that exist.
3. A dialog opened by the script's own element.click() or mouse_click() hangs in that click call first (verified), so in that pattern the Q2 methods are never reached.
4. Recovery: Page.handleJavaScriptDialog returns 'No dialog is showing' unless Page.enable was sent before the dialog opened, and a late Page.enable gets no reply (verified). Navigating away with tab.get closes the dialog and DOM calls work again (verified).
5. Keepalive never ends the wait: pongs come from the browser process and PING_TIMEOUT is 900 s. Only the mechanism is assumed; the connection itself was verified still usable after 34 s, longer than the 20 s ping_interval.
6. Not Python-version dependent (an unbounded await on a never-completed Future); I ran 3.13 only.
7. For A11.4, the overrun is at most click_delay plus one check_input; with the defaults and an immediate find it is about 0.03 s.
8. For A5.7, the busy spin is limited by the timeout; the real bug is that timeout<=0 makes zero attempts.
9. Each realism rating: the main hang is medium (pages with load or timer alerts are uncommon but real, and #77/#291 shows users hit the same thing in wait_for_ready_state), A5.7 is low-medium, A11.4 is low.

groups.summary: Reproduced every member with my own probes, on real headless Chromium 141 and on a browser-free fake CDP peer. (1) Browser._stop awaits Target.detachFromTarget (inside Connection.aclose, connection.py:517) and Browser.close (browser.py:883), and neither has a timeout. A frozen or unresponsive browser therefore makes stop() hang forever before it reaches terminate/kill. Bounding stop() with wait_for leaves the process alive and the profile on disk, and the atexit hook has already been unregistered, so nothing cleans up later. (2) If Chrome dies just before stop(), Connection.aclose raises ConnectionClosedError, because it only catches ProtocolException. The exception aborts _stop: _process stays set, the process is never reaped and the profile leaks. (3) Two concurrent stop() calls race in the terminate/poll loop and one raises AttributeError 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'poll' at _stop:901. (4) Under asyncio.run, the atexit cleanup always fails at `await asyncio.to_thread(self._process.wait)` (_stop:909) with RuntimeError('Executor shutdown has been called'), so the /tmp/uc_* profile leaks. This happens on Python 3.13 and 3.11, and also on the Ctrl+C path. Tab.close() also hangs well past the 10 s its docstring promises, stuck at Tab.close:1079 -> Connection.send.

After cancelling: proc alive True, profile exists True, not in registry. r_sigstop_exit.py: wait_for(stop(),5) timed out; after asyncio.run (atexit hooks ran) proc alive True state T, profile exists True. After wait_for times out, nothing kills Chrome at exit: atexit is unregistered and the instance is gone from the registry, so the process stays alive and the profile stays on disk after asyncio.run returns. I did not test the stderr-pipe variant (separate finding).

With a 0.5 s delay, stop succeeded and the profile was removed. A deterministic fake peer (detach_abort: transport.abort() on Target.detachFromTarget) gave the same ConnectionClosedError, with the process still running and the profile on disk. The frozen-Chrome half is confirmed by the SIGSTOP repro. Extra: in the tabclose run, the atexit callback also failed with 'no close frame received or sent' after Chrome was killed, which left a zombie (state Z) and the profile.

Real Chromium r_concurrent.py: gather(b.stop(), b.stop()) with no stagger gave ['None','None'] in 8 of 8 runs. With the second call staggered by a random 0-0.4 s, 7 of 12 runs gave AttributeError('NoneType' object has no attribute 'poll') @ stop:872->_stop:901. A deterministic fake (a process that exits 0.4 s after SIGTERM, second stop() 0.1 s later) raised AttributeError 3 of 3 times on Python 3.13, and also on 3.11. The surviving stop() still removed the profile, so the bug is the crash. The 'profile cleanup skipped' part does not cause a leak in practice.

r_atexit.py plain: asyncio.run(main) where main starts the browser and never stops it. Output: 'Unhandled exception in asyncio atexit callback <bound method Browser._atexit_cleanup ...>: Executor shutdown has been called' and then 'temp profile exists: True'. The tb mode traceback: _atexit_cleanup:237 -> _stop:909 to_thread -> run_in_executor -> _check_default_executor -> RuntimeError. The same failure occurs in ctx mode (async with await zd.start(): __aexit__ does not stop the browser) and in sigint mode (Ctrl+C). It also reproduces on Python 3.11.17. The Chrome process itself was terminated and reaped; only the profile leaks.

Same root cause and same evidence as A3.1. The profile leaks on every asyncio.run exit without stop() (3 of 3 modes on 3.13, plus 3.11). The `_cleanup_temporary_profile()` call in _atexit_cleanup is skipped because _stop raised first.

groups.refinements:
- Root cause 1 (hang) has two independent unbounded awaits: the per-target Connection.aclose -> Target.detachFromTarget at connection.py:517, and Browser.close at browser.py:883. Either one alone hangs stop(), as the fake peer shows for each. A fix must bound both, or bound _stop's CDP phase as a whole, and must always fall through to terminate/kill. Tab.close has the same unbounded send at tab.py:1079 (Tab.close).
- Root cause 2: Connection.aclose's session branch catches only ProtocolException. Because the listener fails pending transactions with the ConnectionClosed instance itself (listener_loop, _fail_pending_transactions(e)), ConnectionClosedError escapes. It aborts _stop before Browser.close, proxy-forwarder close, terminate/reap and profile removal. The same exception also breaks the atexit path when Chrome has died (seen in the tabclose run: 'Unhandled exception in asyncio atexit callback ...: no close frame received or sent', leaving a zombie and the profile).
- A3.11: the race needs the two stop() calls to be offset (a stagger above a few ms). Simultaneous gather calls rarely hit it on real Chromium (0 of 8). The surviving call still removes the profile, so the impact is a spurious AttributeError, not a leak.
- A3.1/B16.3: only the profile leaks. The process is terminated and reaped by the poll loop before the to_thread call fails. `async with await zd.start()` does not stop the browser in __aexit__, so the documented examples always rely on this broken atexit path.
- stop() calls asyncio_atexit.unregister before _stop, so any hang or exception in _stop leaves nothing to clean up at exit.

groups.summary: I could not refute any member. All of them reproduce on real headless Chromium (Python 3.13.16, websockets 14.1). Q3 is really four separate defects in Browser.stop()/_stop()/_atexit_cleanup, and their realism differs a lot. (1) The atexit leak is deterministic and the most realistic. Under asyncio.run, _stop() reaches `await asyncio.to_thread(self._process.wait)` after Runner.close has already called shutdown_default_executor, gets RuntimeError('Executor shutdown has been called'), and skips _cleanup_temporary_profile. This hits every script that never calls stop(), including Ctrl+C. (2) The stop() hang needs the browser process itself to be wedged. Target.detachFromTarget (sent from Connection.aclose) and Browser.close are sent with no timeout, and both come before the terminate/kill fallback. If the caller bounds stop() with wait_for, Chrome is orphaned and the profile is left, because stop() unregistered the atexit hook first. (3) Connection.aclose catches only ProtocolException. A ConnectionClosedError escapes and aborts _stop when stop() starts before the listener has seen the socket close. (4) Concurrent stop() calls race on self._process and one of them raises AttributeError. The other call still cleans up.

groups.refinements: Treat Q3 as four bugs that share one function. (a) Atexit leak: deterministic on Python 3.10+ (Runner.close calls shutdown_default_executor before loop.close) for any browser not stopped explicitly, including after Ctrl+C. Only the temp profile leaks plus the stderr message: Chrome is terminated and reaped. (b) Hang: only when the browser (main) process stops servicing DevTools: SIGSTOP or a frozen container/VM, a hung browser UI/IO thread, or a remote browser behind a silent network partition. A busy or infinite-looping renderer does NOT trigger it (verified). The stderr-pipe deadlock trigger is unlikely with the default flags, since only about 5 KB is written at startup (verified in this container). The keepalive bounds the wait at about 930 s, but stop() then raises ConnectionClosedError from aclose and still never terminates or kills Chrome. Cancelling stop() via wait_for orphans Chrome and the profile, because the atexit hook is already unregistered. (c) ConnectionClosedError escape: only if stop() starts before the listener has handled the socket close, i.e. within about 3-10 ms of browser death or after blocking synchronous work. A second stop() recovers. (d) Concurrent stop(): about 1 in 10 runs, only a spurious AttributeError in one caller, no leak. A fix must keep the healthy-path stop() fast and without kill (existing test asserts under 2 s and no kill).

groups.summary: I could not disprove any member; I reproduced all four failure modes in Browser._stop on the repo code. (1) An unresponsive browser makes stop() hang forever. The target.aclose() loop (Target.detachFromTarget, Connection.aclose:517) and the Browser.close send (_stop:883) have no timeout and run before terminate/kill. stop() has already unregistered the atexit hook (stop:870), so cancelling it with wait_for leaks the process and the profile. (2) If Chrome dies just before stop(), ConnectionClosedError escapes Connection.aclose (it only catches ProtocolException) and aborts _stop before terminate and profile cleanup. (3) Two stop() calls a little apart crash: one sets self._process=None while the other is in asyncio.sleep(0.25) and then calls self._process.poll() (_stop:901). (4) On the atexit path under asyncio.run, `await asyncio.to_thread(self._process.wait)` (_stop:909) raises RuntimeError('Executor shutdown has been called'), so the temp profile is left behind. A minimal fix in browser.py alone (about 30 lines) fixes all four. All 7 regression tests fail on the repo code and pass on the prototype under Python 3.13 and 3.11. The repo's own tests/core suite passes on the prototype, and mypy shows no new errors.

fix_assessment.diff_summary: zendriver/core/browser.py only (full diff in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-zendriver/b2021b39-94e6-5220-9e66-7f33c0314a80/scratchpad/verify/Q3-fixsafety/fix.diff). (a) New module constant STOP_COMMAND_TIMEOUT = 5 (could be private). (b) _stop: replace `for target in self.targets: await target.aclose()` with `await asyncio.wait_for(asyncio.gather(*(t.aclose() for t in self.targets), return_exceptions=True), STOP_COMMAND_TIMEOUT)` inside `except asyncio.TimeoutError: logger.debug(...)`. This gives one budget for all targets, and per-target exceptions such as ConnectionClosedError are swallowed. (c) Wrap the Browser.close send in asyncio.wait_for(..., STOP_COMMAND_TIMEOUT); the existing broad except already covers the timeout. (d) Snapshot `process = self._process` and use the local for terminate/poll/kill, so a concurrent stop() setting self._process=None cannot break this one. (e) Remove `await asyncio.to_thread(self._process.wait)`: the break path is already reaped by poll(), and after kill() it uses `while process.poll() is None: await asyncio.sleep(0.05)`, which needs no default executor. (f) stop(): call `await self._stop()` first, then asyncio_atexit.unregister and registry discard, so a stop() that fails or is cancelled keeps the atexit fallback.
fix_assessment.risks: No locks are added, so there are no re-entrancy, deadlock or lock-ordering concerns. Cancellation still propagates: wait_for/gather re-raise CancelledError. Each aclose calls _detach_session() synchronously before its send, so a timeout leaves local session state consistent, and Connection.aclose() later fails or clears any pending browser-connection transactions. Behaviour changes callers would notice: (1) stop() of a hung browser now returns after about 23 s with a 'Could not send the close command' warning instead of hanging; (2) detaches run concurrently rather than one after another; (3) gather(return_exceptions=True) drops exceptions other than ProtocolException from aclose without logging them (suggest debug-logging the results); (4) after a stop() that fails or is cancelled, the atexit callback and its strong reference to the Browser stay until loop close, where _atexit_cleanup retries. That is intended, but it is new. (5) A slow but healthy Chrome that takes more than 5 s to answer Browser.close now gets terminate() early. On POSIX that is a graceful SIGTERM. On Windows terminate() is TerminateProcess, but it was already called right after the reply, so this is no worse. The post-kill poll loop is unbounded, like the old wait() (only matters for a D-state process). Python 3.10 compatibility: only wait_for, gather and asyncio.TimeoutError are used. I tested 3.13 and 3.11, not 3.10. Healthy-path stop time is unchanged (0.37 s), and the repo's test_browser_stop_exits_gracefully_without_kill still passes.

groups.summary: Confirmed on real headless Chromium and with browser-free tests. When the renderer stops answering (an open alert()), find, select, find_all, select_all, wait_for, tab(), xpath, cf_is_interactive_challenge_present and verify_cf all hang forever. Each loop checks its timeout only after an unbounded CDP await returns. On a page with a busy main thread they overrun the timeout by the length of the busy period. verify_cf also overruns by up to click_delay. xpath(timeout<=0) never makes an attempt, and with a positive timeout it busy-loops. The triage fix (wrap each loop in asyncio.wait_for(..., timeout), as #291 did) cures the hang but is NOT safe as written: it causes three confirmed regressions. A safer minimal-local variant was prototyped. It also needs a one-line companion fix in Connection._register_handlers, whose bare `except:` swallows the timeout's CancelledError and leaves the call hanging and uncancellable.

fix_assessment.diff_summary:
Diffs are in tab_final.diff, cloudflare_final.diff and connection_v3.diff in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-zendriver/b2021b39-94e6-5220-9e66-7f33c0314a80/scratchpad/verify/Q2-fixsafety/ (the strict-wrap variant for comparison is in .../pkg).
(1) tab.py: new module helper _poll_with_timeout(poll, timeout, message). If timeout <= 0 it awaits poll unbounded, which keeps the single attempt. Otherwise it runs asyncio.wait_for(poll, timeout + 0.5) and turns asyncio.TimeoutError into asyncio.TimeoutError(message).
(2) find, select, find_all and select_all keep their loops unchanged inside a nested _poll() and return await _poll_with_timeout(...). The 0.5 s sleep is clamped to min(0.5, deadline - now), so the last attempt happens at the deadline and the 0.5 s grace lets it finish.
(3) wait_for: same wrap, and it sleeps only after a miss (a strict bound would cut the trailing sleep and throw away an element already found).
(4) xpath: a while-True _poll that always makes at least one attempt, stops when items are found or elapsed >= timeout, sleeps with the same clamp instead of busy-looping, and returns [] on the bound.
(5) cloudflare.py: cf_wait_for_interactive_challenge wraps its scan loop in asyncio.wait_for(_poll(), timeout + 0.5) and returns (None, None, None) on timeout. verify_cf moves the click phase verbatim into _cf_click_challenge(...), bounded by asyncio.wait_for(..., time left + 0.5). On the bound it raises builtin TimeoutError (needed for 3.10) with the existing 'timeout during clicks' message. asyncio.sleep(click_delay) is clamped to the deadline.
(6) connection.py:709: `except:` becomes `except Exception:` in Connection._register_handlers, so a timeout's CancelledError is no longer swallowed.
fix_assessment.risks:
(a) The triage hypothesis, a strict asyncio.wait_for(loop, timeout) as in #291, is unsafe as written:
- wait_for(..., <=0) never runs the attempt. That breaks timeout=0 one-shot checks, and xpath's internal find_all(xpath, timeout=0) would then always return [].
- It cuts the trailing 0.5 s sleep, so the last attempt is lost. Confirmed on Chromium: elements appearing 0.3 s into timeout=0.5, or 0.7 s into timeout=1, are found by the repo but get TimeoutError with the strict wrap.
- wait_for's sleep after a hit gets cut, so an element it already found is discarded.
The prototype avoids all three with the timeout<=0 bypass, a grace of one poll interval, clamped sleeps and no sleep after a hit.
(b) The companion fix in Connection._register_handlers is required. Without it, a pending domain enable (a handler registered while the page is blocked) makes the call hang and become uncancellable, and the same applies to the existing wait_for_ready_state fix.
(c) Behaviour changes callers may notice:
- A blocked page now raises or returns at timeout+0.5 s instead of hanging.
- wait_for and tab() return as soon as the element is found (no 0.5 s trailing sleep) and give up at about timeout instead of timeout+0.5.
- The last find/select attempt happens at the deadline instead of up to 0.5 s after it.
- xpath polls every 0.5 s instead of spinning (13 vs 1272 sends in 0.5 s), so an element can be found up to 0.5 s later. timeout<=0 now makes one attempt and can return elements where it used to return [].
- verify_cf's click_delay sleeps are clamped to the deadline, so solves that were only detected after the deadline now raise TimeoutError, as the docstring says they should.
(d) timeout<=0 deliberately keeps one unbounded attempt, so it still hangs on a blocked renderer, as query_selector does.
(e) Cancellation side effects (the same as with #291):
- xpath cancelled between DOM.enable and disable leaves the DOM agent enabled.
- A cancelled performSearch leaves a search session open in the browser.
- A cancelled Transaction stays in mapper until Chrome replies (verified it drains once the dialog is dismissed).
- A cancelled first-time _attach_session can leak a browser-side session.
(f) No lock is held across the bounded region. _open_lock and _attach_lock are released by `async with` on cancel, and the helper takes no lock, so there is no re-entrancy or deadlock issue. Nested calls are fine: xpath calls find_all(timeout=0) from inside its bounded poll.
(g) Builtin vs asyncio TimeoutError: on 3.10 they differ. verify_cf converts explicitly, and the tab methods keep asyncio.TimeoutError. Verified on 3.10.20, 3.11.17 and 3.13.16.
(h) The 0.5 s grace is a heuristic. A final attempt that takes longer than 0.5 s on a very heavy page is cut, giving TimeoutError where the repo would have returned the result.

groups.summary: Confirmed. Browser.start (zendriver/core/browser.py) launches Chrome with util._start_process and calls util.get_registered_instances().add(self) before it connects. The code after that point has no try/except/finally; it calls stop() only on the `if not self.info` path. Browser.create registers asyncio_atexit only after `await instance.start()` returns. So a cancel (wait_for timeout, task.cancel, Ctrl+C) or an exception from set_discover_targets, update_targets, _wait_for_initial_tab or _read_headless_user_agent leaves three things behind: the Chrome process (reparented to pid 1 after the interpreter exits), the /tmp/uc_* profile, and a permanent registry entry. The caller never gets the instance, so it cannot stop it. Minimal fix: move the post-registration body into a helper and wrap the call in `except BaseException: stop(); raise`. In attach mode (host+port) the handler must close only the connection: a plain stop() would send Browser.close and shut down the user's existing browser.

fix_assessment.diff_summary: zendriver/core/browser.py, Browser.start: after `util.get_registered_instances().add(self)`, the rest of start() moves unchanged into a new `async def _connect(self, connect_existing: bool) -> None` (its trailing `return self` is removed). start() now does `try: await self._connect(connect_existing) except BaseException: if connect_existing and self.connection: await self.connection.aclose()  # do not close a browser that was not launched here; await self.stop(); raise` and then `return self`. stop() is idempotent: the second call made after the existing 'Failed to connect' path returns early, and asyncio_atexit.unregister of a callback that was never registered is a no-op. Browser.create is unchanged.
fix_assessment.risks: No locks are on the start/stop path (_update_target_info_mutex is used only in _handle_target_update), so there is no re-entrancy or lock-ordering risk. Behaviour changes callers would notice: (a) wait_for(zd.start(), T) now raises only after cleanup completes, about 0.25s later with a Chrome that honours SIGTERM (measured T=0.05 gave 0.30s; 3s hangs gave 3.3-3.4s), and up to about 3s more plus kill if Chrome ignores SIGTERM. (b) A Chrome launched by zendriver gets Browser.close on a failed start. (c) In attach mode the connection is closed but the remote browser is left running, and the instance is unregistered. (d) A user who calls `await browser.start()` directly and handles the failure gets an already-stopped instance; calling stop() again is a harmless no-op, and start() can be retried because _process is cleared. Residual risks: a second cancel during cleanup leaves the temp profile (the process is already SIGTERMed); an exception raised inside stop() would replace the original exception or CancelledError (suggest suppressing Exception from the cleanup with a debug log); GeneratorExit via coro.close() now produces RuntimeError('coroutine ignored GeneratorExit'); in attach mode a cancel before the connection exists still leaves an empty uc_* temp dir because of _stop's early return. groups.summary: Confirmed on real headless Chromium 141 (Python 3.13). util._start_process (util.py:332-355) starts Chrome with stdout=PIPE and stderr=PIPE, and nothing reads them while Chrome runs. The only reader is _read_process_stderr (util.py:358), and it runs only on the connect-failure path in Browser.start (browser.py:588). Once the stderr pipe is full, Chrome's logging thread blocks in anon_pipe_write and CDP stops answering. This happens with --enable-logging=stderr after about 44 console.log calls, and with DEFAULT flags after about 183 navigations that fail the TLS handshake (about 288 B of ERROR log each). A minimal local fix works: stdout=DEVNULL, plus a daemon thread that drains stderr and keeps only the last 64 KiB, which _read_process_stderr then returns. The browser-free regression tests fail on the repo code and pass on the prototype, the repo's real-browser tests pass on the prototype, and mypy reports no new errors.

fix_assessment.diff_summary: zendriver/core/util.py only, diff saved at /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-zendriver/b2021b39-94e6-5220-9e66-7f33c0314a80/scratchpad/verify/Q5-fixsafety/fix.diff. (1) _start_process passes stdout=subprocess.DEVNULL instead of PIPE; stdin and stderr stay PIPE. After Popen it registers _stderr_tails[process] = _StderrTail(process.stderr). (2) New class _StderrTail: a daemon thread named 'zendriver-browser-stderr' loops `while chunk := os.read(stream.fileno(), 2**16)`, appends under a threading.Lock and trims with `del self._data[:-size]`, so at most 64 KiB is kept. It closes the stream itself at EOF and catches OSError/ValueError. Its async read(n, timeout) runs `await asyncio.to_thread(self._thread.join, timeout)` (0.25 s, the same budget as before) and returns the last n bytes. (3) Module-level `_stderr_tails: weakref.WeakKeyDictionary[Popen[bytes], _StderrTail]`. (4) _read_process_stderr returns the tail decoded with errors='replace' when the process is tracked. Untracked processes still go through the old read path. browser.py is unchanged.
fix_assessment.risks:
Behaviour changes: (a) browser._process.stdout is now None; it was an unread pipe. (b) browser._process.stderr is now consumed by the drain thread, so a user reading it directly would race with the thread. Both attributes are private. (c) The failure log may now contain up to 64 KiB of Chrome noise, such as dbus errors, at INFO level; before, it said 'No output' for a live Chrome. (d) Chrome's stderr is still discarded during the session apart from the tail; forwarding it to logger.debug would be an optional addition.

Concurrency: one threading.Lock, held only for append/trim and the final copy. It is never held across an await, nothing else locks inside it, and no asyncio.Lock is involved, so there is no re-entrancy or lock-ordering hazard.

Cancel path: if Browser.start is cancelled during _read_process_stderr, the executor's join finishes within 0.25 s on its own. This is harmless.

Lifetime: one thread per launched browser, which exits at EOF once Chrome and its crashpad/zygote children exit; I verified this after stop(). An orphaned child that keeps the write end open keeps one daemon thread and one fd alive until it exits. The thread keeps its own reference to the stream and checks fileno() on every iteration, so the fd is not closed by GC and reused under it. Only an external process.stderr.close() racing with an in-flight read has a tiny window. If thread start fails (RuntimeError under resource exhaustion), Popen has already spawned Chrome, which is then orphaned; this edge case could be guarded.

Compatibility: no new mypy errors (332 errors in both the untouched and the prototype trees, all in cdp/; util.py reports 'Success: no issues found'). The code works on Python 3.10+ (walrus; annotation-only generic subscript under `from __future__ import annotations`; tested on 3.11 and 3.13), and os.read on the pipe fd also works on Windows.

Alternatives considered: DEVNULL-only would regress the exited-Chrome diagnostics that work today (test_stderr_of_an_exited_browser_is_read passes on the repo code). A temp file grows without bound under --enable-logging --v=1, and /tmp is often tmpfs.

groups.refinements:
- Effective capacity is 16 pipe pages, not 64 KiB of bytes. With small lines Chrome blocks at about 63-64 KB. With lines just over 2 KB it blocks at about 37 KB, because each write takes its own page.
- What hangs depends on which Chrome process logs first once the pipe is full:
  - Browser process (--enable-logging console messages): everything, including Browser.getVersion and stop(). stop() sits on Target.detachFromTarget with no timeout; that belongs to the stop() group.
  - GPU process (WebGL): rendering-dependent tab operations (tab.get, evaluate on that tab, screenshot). Browser.getVersion, new_tab and stop() keep working.
  - Network service (TLS errors): navigation and network only.
  Each process blocks only when it next logs, so the set of stuck operations grows over time.
- Default-flag triggers are per-event ERROR logs, not volume:
  - Each WebGL context in a GPU-less environment (Docker/CI/servers): about 390 B headless, about 136 B headful/Xvfb, so roughly 155 or roughly 440 such page loads.
  - Each failing TLS handshake: about 170 B.
  - console.log, normal pages, 404s, DNS failures and connection refused add nothing.
  - Idle growth is negligible (about 1.8 KB per 10 min).
  On a desktop with a real GPU the WebGL line is probably not emitted (assumed).
- With --enable-logging=stderr (a common debugging flag) the hang comes within seconds.
- stdout received 0 bytes in every run, so only stderr matters in practice. stdin=PIPE is harmless.
- Draining fully recovers Chrome, so a drain or a file is a complete fix.
- Python-version independent (kernel pipe semantics); I only ran 3.13.
- Windows release Chrome does not log to stderr without --enable-logging (assumed), so Linux (and probably macOS) is the main exposure.
- B13.8 applies only when Chrome is still alive at the failure: DevTools port race, or startup slower than about 2.5 s (default 10 x 0.25 s). The canonical root-without-sandbox and crash-at-start failures exit, hit EOF and are reported correctly. Its impact is a missing diagnostic line, which I rate cosmetic; the group's severity stays hang.

groups.summary: Confirmed on Python 3.12 and 3.13, not on 3.11. In BaseRequestExpectation._request_handler (zendriver/core/expect.py, around lines 37-45) the code runs `self._remove_request_handler(); self.request_id = event.request_id; self.request_future.set_result(event)` with no done() guard. On 3.12+, Listener.listener_loop (connection.py, around lines 922-1016) drains buffered messages without yielding: wait_for no longer creates a task, and both asyncio.Queue.get on the flat-session inbox and websockets 14.1 recv return at once. It calls asyncio.create_task(callback(ev)) for every matching RequestWillBeSent before the first task runs and removes the handler. The first task resolves request_future with R1. Each later task overwrites request_id with Rn, then raises InvalidStateError, which nobody retrieves. From then on _response_handler and _loading_finished_handler match Rn. Result: .request/.value (RequestExpectation) describe R1, while .response, ResponseExpectation.value, response_body and loading_finished describe Rn. BaseFetchInterception._response_handler and DownloadExpectation._handler hit the same lost InvalidStateError on a burst; they keep the first event, so their result is still right.

groups.refinements: Python-version dependent: reproduces only on Python >= 3.12 (3.12.3 and 3.13.16 tested). On 3.11, wait_for wraps each receive in a new task, so the loop yields between messages and the first handler task runs and unregisters before the next event is dispatched (0/20 real-browser trials, 0 fake-peer mismatches). Both receive paths trigger it on 3.12+: the flat-session asyncio.Queue inbox (real Chromium tab) and the owned-websocket recv (fake peer Connection). The wrong request is the last matching request in the same buffered burst, not always the page's last request. Root cause in expect.py: _request_handler mutates request_id before set_result and never checks request_future.done(). The fix should check done() before any mutation; a set_result guard alone is not enough. For BaseFetchInterception._response_handler (intercept.py ~35-42) and DownloadExpectation._handler (expect.py ~206-208), the only wrong effect is the lost InvalidStateError task: the first event is still the one returned. Unrelated observation outside the group: when page JS never reads a fetch() body, Chromium sent no Network.loadingFinished for it within 10 s, so response_body (which has no timeout) blocks.

groups.summary: I could not refute this. On Python 3.12 and 3.13, when several Network.requestWillBeSent events that match the pattern are waiting in the inbox at once, Listener.listener_loop dispatches them back-to-back without yielding. It calls asyncio.create_task(_request_handler(ev)) once per event before the first task runs and calls _remove_request_handler(). The first task resolves request_future with R1. Each later task then overwrites self.request_id (BaseRequestExpectation._request_handler, expect.py:44) and fails on set_result with InvalidStateError, which nobody retrieves. From then on _response_handler and _loading_finished_handler match the last request (Rn). So .request/.value describe R1 while .response, ResponseExpectation.value and .response_body describe Rn. Reproduced on real headless Chromium and on a fake peer, on 3.12 and 3.13. No mismatch on 3.11.

Code path (read fresh):

- Keepalive or timeouts do not matter: this is a wrong result, not a wait.

groups.refinements:
1. Only on Python >= 3.12. Verified: 3.11 never reproduced (real or fake peer). On 3.10 and 3.11, wait_for wraps the receive in a new task and yields once per message, so the first handler task runs and removes itself before the next event is dispatched.

2. It needs at least 2 pattern-matching RequestWillBeSent events that are queued in the session inbox at the same time (same read burst). Spacing the frames 20 ms apart removes it. Exact-URL patterns never trigger it. Broad regexes plus parallel subresources or fetches trigger it almost every time (7/8 to 100%).

3. ResponseExpectation.value alone still returns a genuine matching response, just not the first. The harm is visible when code pairs .request/.value with .response/.response_body, or relies on 'first match'.

4. Extra consequence: if the last match in the burst never gets a response (failed, cancelled or blocked), exp.response and response_body hang forever, although the first match completed. Verified with the fake peer.

5. Every burst also leaves 'Task exception was never retrieved' InvalidStateError log noise.

6. The side claims about BaseFetchInterception and DownloadExpectation InvalidStateError were not reproduced. My real-Chromium intercept probe on 8 images logged 0 lost errors, so Fetch.requestPaused events apparently do not arrive in the same burst there. A done() guard would still be harmless there.

7. Not this group, but noticed while testing: Chrome sent no Network.loadingFinished for a fetch whose body JS never read (within 2 s), so response_body waits forever for such fetches regardless of this race.

groups.summary: Confirmed, deterministic, and the same on Python 3.11 and 3.13. Connection._register_handlers (connection.py:669-720) copies self.enabled_domains at the start. If it then has to auto-enable a new domain, it awaits self.send(domain.enable(), _is_update=True). That nested send still calls aopen(), and aopen() runs _register_handlers again. The nested call removes the stale auto-enabled domain (one with no handlers left, e.g. network) from self.enabled_domains. When the outer call resumes, its final loop `for ed in enabled_domains: self.enabled_domains.remove(ed)` (line 720) removes that domain a second time, outside any try, and raises ValueError: list.remove(x): x not in list. The error comes out of send -> aopen (line 458) -> _register_handlers, so the user's command is never sent. The new domain's X.enable has already gone out, so state converges to [new domain] and the next send works.

groups.refinements:
1. Version scope: through Listener.listener_loop the bug only shows on Python >= 3.12. There, asyncio.wait_for no longer creates a task, and both websockets' recv() and the session asyncio.Queue.get() return buffered data without suspending. Severity is still wrong-result, and on 3.12+ it is easy to hit: any pattern that matches several resources of one page.
2. Fix-form refinement: do not use the triage's `if self.request_future.done(): return`. A timed-out `asyncio.wait_for(exp.value, t)` cancels request_future itself (verified on 3.11 and 3.13). After that, the triage guard means no later match ever sets request_id, so `exp.response` and `response_body` hang. The repo code still resolves them, though it logs an InvalidStateError. I built that variant at .../Q6-fixsafety/alt; it fails test_response_still_resolves_after_timed_out_wait_for_request with a timeout. Instead, guard on `self.request_id is not None` and make every set_result conditional on `not future.done()`.
3. Sibling: BaseFetchInterception._response_handler in intercept.py has the same unguarded set_result. Adding `if not self.response_future.done()` there is safe. Extra paused requests stay paused until teardown's fetch.disable either way, so that guard changes nothing users would see.
4. A dispatch-time check in Listener (skip callbacks that are no longer registered) would change semantics for all user handlers. It is not needed here.

fix_assessment.diff_summary:
zendriver/core/expect.py only (full diff at .../Q6-fixsafety/prototype.diff).
- BaseRequestExpectation._request_handler: returns early when `self.request_id is not None` (comment: matching events dispatched before the handler removed itself must not replace the tracked request), and wraps set_result in `if not self.request_future.done()`.
- _response_handler and _loading_finished_handler: still remove themselves on a request_id match; only set_result is guarded by `if not <future>.done()`.

fix_assessment.risks:
- Locking and cancellation: no locks are involved and the handlers contain no awaits, so there are no re-entrancy, lock-ordering or cancellation-path concerns.
- Behaviour change: after the first match, later matching requests in the same burst are ignored (intended), and no InvalidStateError tasks are logged any more.
- Cancelled future: if request_future was cancelled by a timed-out wait on exp.value, the first later match still sets request_id, so exp.response and response_body keep working as before.
- Not fixed (pre-existing): handler tasks created before `reset()` that run after it can still match into the new futures. Fixing that needs a generation token.
- Coverage gaps: intercept.py's BaseFetchInterception._response_handler is unpatched; it needs the same one-line set_result guard. The end-to-end test only fails on Python >= 3.12 (it passes on 3.11 repo code). The two direct double-dispatch tests and the cancel-edge test fail on 3.11 repo code too, so the suite still catches regressions on every supported version.

groups.refinements: Trigger conditions: (1) every handler of an auto-enabled domain X is removed; expect_request/expect_response handlers remove themselves when they match, and teardown removes the rest; (2) a handler is added for a domain Y that is in neither enabled_domains nor manually_enabled_domains and is not target/storage; Y must also have an enable() command, since a domain without one raises AttributeError before any nested send; (3) the next send on that connection is the first one after both changes. If any send runs between the removal and the addition, X is dropped cleanly and the bug does not trigger. For example, awaiting response_body inside expect_response sends Network.getResponseBody, which cleans up X. The race does not depend on timing or Python version: the nested pass finishes inside the awaited call chain before the outer pass resumes, so the order is forced. Any tab command can be the trigger (evaluate, reload, navigate via browser.get on an existing tab). Internal handlers (Browser.get TargetInfoChanged, Tab.close TargetDestroyed) use the target domain, which is skipped, so zendriver cannot trigger this by itself; user handlers are required. Impact is bounded: one ValueError, the command is dropped, enabled_domains converges to the correct list, and the next send works. No hang, nothing left inconsistent.

groups.summary: Confirmed. Connection._register_handlers takes a copy of self.enabled_domains, then awaits send(domain_mod.enable(), _is_update=True) for any handler domain that is not enabled yet. That nested send calls aopen(), and aopen() always runs _register_handlers again (connection.py, aopen ~L458). The nested pass prunes the stale auto-enabled domain from the live list. When the outer pass resumes, its final loop calls `self.enabled_domains.remove(ed)` (~L720) for that same domain. The call is outside any try, so it raises ValueError: list.remove(x): x not in list. The error comes out of send() -> aopen(), before the user's Transaction is even created. So the user's command never reaches the wire (only Log.enable/Page.enable does), and no tx is left in mapper. The bug is deterministic and reproduces with public APIs on real headless Chromium: add_handler/remove_handlers followed by evaluate, and expect_request followed by add_handler(page.LoadEventFired) and reload. The next send succeeds because the state has converged. Minimal fix: guard the final removal with `if ed in self.enabled_domains:`.

fix_assessment.diff_summary: zendriver/core/_contradict.py, ContraDict.__getattribute__: `if attribute in self:` becomes `if attribute in self and not hasattr(type(self), attribute):`, with a 2-line comment. Keys that collide with a real class attribute then fall through to the existing code: _check_key, then getattr(super(), attribute) for dict-method names, or object.__getattribute__ for data descriptors such as __class__. Keys that are not class attributes (id, class, data-id, Items, title) are still returned as attributes, so that behaviour is unchanged.
fix_assessment.risks: No locks or async code are involved, so there are no re-entrancy, lock-ordering or cancel-path concerns. hasattr(type(self), name) goes through type.__getattribute__ on the class, so it cannot recurse into the instance hook, and it runs only when the name is already a key. Behaviour change callers could notice: cd.items, elem.attrs.clear, get_js_attributes().clear and similar now return the dict method instead of the stored value. The docstring and the _warning_names_message both document that, so code relying on the old result was relying on the bug. The values stay reachable via cd['items'], elem.get('items'), elem['items'] and elem.items (through Element.__getattr__). Remaining unchanged edge: dunder keys that are non-data descriptors (e.g. '__len__', '__init__', '__doc__') still shadow through object.__getattribute__, because the instance __dict__ is the dict itself. This is unrealistic for HTML attributes and was already the behaviour. mypy: 332 errors on both the prototype and an untouched copy, the diff of the two logs is identical, all errors are in zendriver/cdp/, and there are none in _contradict.py or element.py. The repo's tab/browser/cloudflare/frames/keyinputs suites pass 69/69 on both copies with headless Chromium. That covers Browser.info (a ContraDict read via .webSocketDebuggerUrl), which every browser start uses. Avoid the naive reorder variant, because it regresses getattr access for 'class', hyphenated keys and case variants of the warning names.

groups.summary: Confirmed. Browser.__aexit__ (browser.py:837-841) and Connection.__aexit__ (connection.py:593-599, which Tab inherits) both do `if exc_type and exc_val: raise exc_type(exc_val)` instead of returning None. I reproduced it three ways: against a fake CDP peer, against an unstarted Browser instance, and against real headless Chromium (Python 3.13.16, websockets 14.1). Any exception whose constructor needs more than one argument turns into TypeError: JSONDecodeError, UnicodeDecodeError, websockets ConnectionClosedError, and ExceptionGroup from a failing TaskGroup, so `except*` no longer matches. ProtocolException comes back as a new object with code=None and '[code: -32000]' folded into its message. KeyError('k') becomes KeyError(KeyError('k')). sys.exit(3) inside the block makes the process exit with status 1 and print '3'. A control context manager whose __aexit__ returns None passes every original exception object through unchanged. Browser.__aexit__ also never stops the browser: browser.stopped stays False and the Chrome pid is still alive after the block.

groups.refinements: Saying the traceback is 'lost' overstates it. Because the new exception is raised inside __aexit__, the original is kept as __context__, and default printing shows it under 'During handling of the above exception, another exception occurred'. What actually changes is the type and identity of the exception the caller catches, plus its attributes, and its __traceback__ now points at __aexit__. This is not specific to a Python version (ExceptionGroup/TaskGroup cases need 3.11+; the JSONDecodeError and ProtocolException cases hit on every supported version). Connection.__aexit__ does call aclose() before re-raising. Browser.__aexit__ never calls stop(), so a separate question is whether it should. The suggested fix (just return None and let Python re-raise the original) is confirmed by my control context manager, which passes every original exception object through unchanged.

fix_assessment.diff_summary:
zendriver/core/tab.py, Tab.wait_for_ready_state. Before `async def _poll()` add:
    # document.readyState only moves forward, so a later state also means
    # the requested one was reached
    states = ("loading", "interactive", "complete")
    reached = states[states.index(until) :]
and in _poll change `if ready_state == until:` to `if ready_state in reached:`.
The timeout, the error message and the evaluate-hang handling from #291 are unchanged. ruff format and ruff check are clean. Suggested CHANGELOG Unreleased/Fixed entry: '`Tab.wait_for_ready_state` no longer times out when the page is already past the requested state, such as the default `until="interactive"` on a page that has finished loading'. Optionally add to the docstring that it returns immediately if the page is already in that state or a later one.
fix_assessment.risks:
- Locks and re-entrancy: no locks or shared state are touched, so there is no re-entrancy, deadlock or lock-ordering concern.
- Cancel and error paths: unchanged. The index is computed outside asyncio.wait_for, so the existing timeout still covers evaluate(). A ProtocolException from evaluate (for example a context destroyed during navigation) still propagates as before.
- Unexpected values: None, '' or any other unexpected readyState value is not in `reached`, so polling continues as today. The regression test covers this.
- Invalid `until` (behaviour change): a value outside the Literal, such as 'complet', now raises ValueError from tuple.index immediately instead of polling and then raising TimeoutError. mypy already rejects such values at the call site. If even that change is unwanted, use `reached = states[states.index(until):] if until in states else (until,)`.
- until='loading' (behaviour change): it now returns at once on any document. Code that relied on == to detect a new navigation entering 'loading' after an old 'complete' document would return early, but that was already racy because a 100ms poll can miss the loading phase.
- until='interactive' and other callers: 'interactive' can now be satisfied by a 'complete' document, which is the intended fix. Callers using 'complete' (all in-repo callers and tests) are unaffected; the repo tests that use it pass on the prototype.
- mypy: the prototype and an untouched copy each report 332 pre-existing errors, all path-related in cdp/ modules, with an empty diff. Neither reports any error in core/tab.py, and `uv run mypy` on the repo itself reports no issues.

(1) The bare `except:` in Connection._register_handlers (connection.py:709) catches the CancelledError raised at the nested `await self.send(domain_mod.enable(), _is_update=True)`. The outer send keeps going, re-sends the same X.enable (the handler took the domain back out of enabled_domains, and send's own `await self._register_handlers()` runs again), then sends the real command. A wait_for timeout or task.cancel() is then ignored: the call either returns normally later or hangs for good. Later cancels are swallowed as well. The bare `except:` in Connection._register_handlers (line 709, around `await self.send(domain_mod.enable(), _is_update=True)` at line 707) swallows CancelledError. It then drops the domain from enabled_domains, and the next handler type in the loop, or send()'s second `_register_handlers()` call (line 654), sends Domain.enable again. So while the renderer is blocked, a single wait_for timeout or task.cancel() can never get the call out, and it hangs without limit. If the enable is only slow, the timeout is ignored and the call returns late with a normal result. I reproduced this against real headless Chromium through a documented API (expect_request + Tab.get(timeout=3) on a page with an open alert()), which hung for over 25s; without the handler the same navigation succeeds in 0.11s. SEED-X2 is real but misplaced and low-impact. The bare except is in Element.mouse_click (line 576), not Element.click: Element.click calls flash(0.25) unwrapped and raises TimeoutError correctly. In mouse_click a wait_for timeout or task.cancel() landing in the trailing flash() is turned into a normal return, after the click has already been sent. SEED-X3 is refuted: UpstreamProxy.open_tunnel's `except BaseException` closes the writer and ends with a bare `raise`, so CancelledError propagates.

member_verdicts.note: Fake CDP peer, Python 3.13 and 3.11, Network.enable and Runtime.evaluate never answered: wait_for(conn.send(evaluate), 1) is still running after 6s; task.cancel() also hangs. Stack chain: send:654 -> _register_handlers:707 -> send:662 (await tx on a second Network.enable). Controls: no handler raises TimeoutError at 1.00s; enable answered and evaluate dropped raises TimeoutError at 1.00s. Slow enable (2s) with timeout 1s returns a normal result at 3.00s; Network.enable was sent twice (t=0 and t=1). A second explicit cancel was swallowed too when the retried enable was outstanding. Real Chrome, hung renderer (verified): wait_for(tab.evaluate, 3) with a cdp.network handler is still hung after 40s; control raises TimeoutError at 3.00s. Real Chrome, open alert() (verified): wait_for_ready_state(timeout=3) with a cdp.page handler hangs for over 20s, and `async with tab.expect_request('*'): await tab.get(url, timeout=3)` hangs for over 25s stuck in aopen:458 -> _register_handlers:707 (pending tx: Network.enable). Without a handler, the same tab.get returns in 0.11s. The hang ends only when the connection closes: browser.stop() fails the pending tx with ProtocolException. This was not deliberate: the code dates from the squashed root commit 5c1a005 (nodriver origin), its comment is about tolerating errors, and no test asserts the current behaviour.

Location correction: the bare except is in Element.mouse_click (try: await self.flash() / except: pass, line 576), not Element.click. Element.click awaits flash(0.25) unwrapped (line 432), and the real-Chrome control raised TimeoutError at 1.00s. In real Chrome, with the page making flash()'s script busy for 3s (zendriver itself not patched), wait_for(el.mouse_click(), 1) returned normally at 1.00s with no TimeoutError. With task.cancel() at 1s (stack at Element.flash:992 -> send:662), the task completed normally and the code after the call ran. The page had already received mouseup and click, so the lost signal is a cancel arriving after the real work is done. It is not a hang on its own, but a cancel during flash is silently lost and the task keeps running.

UpstreamProxy.open_tunnel's `except BaseException as e` (line 110) closes the writer, maps only OSError, IncompleteReadError and TimeoutError to ProxyError, and re-raises everything else with a bare `raise`. Against a fake upstream that accepts TCP and never replies, on Python 3.13 and 3.11, for both http and socks5: task.cancel() at 0.5s raised CancelledError at 0.50s, and wait_for(open_tunnel, 0.5) raised TimeoutError at 0.50s. Catching BaseException here is deliberate: it is for cleanup (commit d089840).

groups.refinements: X1: three conditions are needed. (1) A handler exists for a domain that is not yet auto-enabled. expect_request and expect_response create this on every use, because _teardown removes the handlers and the next _register_handlers drops Network from enabled_domains, so the next send re-sends Network.enable. (2) Domain.enable is still outstanding when the timeout or cancel fires, which in practice means the renderer is blocked (open alert/confirm, JS busy loop, long synchronous work). On a responsive page Network.enable answered in 0.00s (verified), so the window is milliseconds. (3) The caller relies on a timeout or cancel; Tab.get (timeout=10) and wait_for_ready_state rely on one internally. When the renderer stays blocked, the call hangs until the connection closes, not just runs late. Websocket keepalive does not bound it: ping_timeout is 900s, and the browser process stays responsive (browser-level CDP verified; pongs assumed). It reproduces on 3.11 and 3.13 (3.10 is assumed to behave like 3.11). Getting out takes one cancel per handler type of the stuck domain plus one, because each swallowed cancel triggers a re-enable. X2: the cancel must land in the trailing flash() of mouse_click (about 2 round trips after the mouse events). The click has already been sent, so the harm is limited to a lost task.cancel() (the task keeps running) or wait_for returning instead of raising. mouse_click's docstring itself says to use click() instead. X3: no defect.
